cards.title: Defining a search problem
cards.hook: Before an agent can search, we must describe the world as states, actions and costs.
cards.visual:
ComponentRomania example
State space20 cities
Initial stateArad
Goal state + goal testBucharest; goal_fun(s) = 1 if s = Bucharest
ACTIONS(s)drive to a connected city
RESULT(s,a)the city you arrive in
Action costroad distance, e.g. cost(A,S) = 140
formula: a fixed sequence of actions from start to goal
the one with the least path cost (e.g. 418 km, not 450 or 733)
example: Two solutions Arad→Bucharest: blue A-S-F-B = 140+99+211 = 450; green A-T-L-M-D-C-P-B = 733.
cards.memory: SIGAT-C: States, Initial, Goal, Actions, Transition, Cost.
cards.trap: The goal TEST is part of the problem; the PATH (sequence of actions) is the solution, not a single state.
explain: A search problem is a precise description of a puzzle so a computer can solve it. Think of planning a road trip: you need to know every city you could be in (states), where you start, where you want to end up, which roads leave each city (actions), where each road takes you (transition model) and how long each road is (cost).

The lecture assumes the world is fully observable (you always know which city you are in), deterministic (a road always leads to the same city) and known (you have the full map). Because nothing is uncertain, the answer is simply a fixed list of moves.

A solution is ANY sequence of actions from the start to the goal. The optimal solution is the one with the smallest total cost. In Romania there are many routes from Arad to Bucharest (450, 733, 418, …); only the 418 km route is optimal.

where: the i-th action (drive along a road)
step cost of doing action a in state s (road length)

cards.title: Frontier, tree search and graph search
cards.hook: Search grows a tree from the start state; the frontier is the to-do list of leaves.
cards.visual:
Tree searchGraph search
Remembers explored states?NoYes (explored set)
Repeated statesPossible (e.g. Arad→Sibiu→Arad)Never re-expanded
Add child if…alwaysnot in frontier or explored
formula: set of leaf nodes = candidates to expand
apply ACTIONS + RESULT to create children, connect them to n
which frontier node to pick next
example: Expand Arad → children Sibiu, Timișoara, Zerind join the frontier.
Expand Sibiu in TREE search → Arad appears again as a child (repeated state).
cards.memory: Tree search has amnesia; graph search keeps a diary (explored set).
cards.trap: In the lecture pseudocode the goal test for tree/graph search, UCS and A* happens when a node is SELECTED for expansion, but the BFS/DFS code tests when a child is GENERATED.
explain: Search algorithms build a search tree. The root is the start state. Expanding a node means asking 'where can I go from here?' and adding every answer as a child.

The frontier is the to-do list: all leaf nodes generated but not yet expanded. Every algorithm in Lecture 2 has the same loop (pick a node from the frontier, test if it is the goal, expand it); they only differ in WHICH node they pick.

Tree search forgets where it has been, so the same city can appear many times (Arad → Sibiu → Arad …). Graph search keeps an explored set and never expands a state twice, which avoids loops and wasted work.

cards.title: BFS vs DFS (uninformed search)
cards.hook: Blind searches use no knowledge of where the goal is.
cards.visual:
BFSDFS
FrontierFIFO queueLIFO stack
Expandsshallowest nodedeepest node
Complete?Yes*No
Cost-optimal?Yes (unit costs: fewest actions)No
TimeO(b^d)O(b^m)
SpaceO(b^d)O(bm)
example: Binary tree A(B(D,E),C(F,G)): BFS order A, B, C, D, E, F, G.
DFS with goal M: A, B, D, H, I, E, J, K, C, F, L, M.
cards.memory: BFS = Breadth = Bread queue (first in line served first). DFS = Dive deep, stack of plates.
cards.trap: DFS uses little memory but returns the FIRST solution it finds, even if it's expensive.
explain: Breadth-first search explores level by level, like ripples on a pond: all nodes 1 step away, then 2 steps away, and so on. It uses a FIFO queue (first in, first out). It always finds the solution with the fewest actions, but it must remember a whole level, so memory grows as bd.

Depth-first search dives down one branch as far as possible before backing up, like exploring a maze by always taking the left-most corridor. It uses a LIFO stack (last in, first out). It needs little memory (one path plus siblings) but it can return an expensive solution and can get lost in infinite branches.
Both are uninformed (blind): they use no estimate of how far the goal is.

tex.t: \text{BFS: time } O(b^d),\; \text{space } O(b^d) \qquad \text{DFS: time } O(b^m),\; \text{space } O(bm)

cards.title: Uniform-cost search (UCS)
cards.hook: UCS always grows the cheapest path so far, like water spreading evenly.
cards.visual:
StepFrontier (node: g)Expand
1Arad:0Arad
2Zerind:75, Timișoara:118, Sibiu:140Zerind
………
k…, Bucharest:418, …Bucharest when it is the lowest
formula: g = exact path cost from the start
when the goal is selected (popped), not when generated
example: From Arad: Zerind 75, Timișoara 118, Sibiu 140 → expand Zerind first (75).
Bucharest is returned with f = g = 418.
cards.trap: Do not stop when Bucharest is first ADDED to the frontier (via Făgăraș, 450); wait until it is popped with the lowest cost (418).
explain: Uniform-cost search always expands the node with the cheapest path so far. Imagine water flowing out from Arad along every road at the same speed: it reaches nearby cities first, and it reaches Bucharest first along the shortest road route.
It keeps the frontier in a priority queue ordered by g(n). It only stops when the goal is taken out of the frontier, not when it is first seen, because a cheaper route might still be waiting.
UCS is complete and cost-optimal, but it has no sense of direction: it expands cities in every direction, even away from the goal.

where: exact cost of the path from the start to node n

cards.title: Greedy best-first search
cards.hook: Greedy runs toward whatever LOOKS closest to the goal and ignores the cost already paid.
cards.visual:
From Aradh(n) = SLD to Bucharest
Sibiu253 ← pick
Timișoara329
Zerind374
then Făgăraș176 ← pick (vs RV 193, Oradea 380)
formula: estimated cost from n to the goal
Not always (graph version on finite spaces: yes)
example: Node A (g=400, h=50) vs node B (g=100, h=80): greedy picks h = 50, ignoring g.
cards.trap: Greedy reaches Bucharest via Făgăraș (cost 450), not the optimal 418.
explain: Greedy best-first search always expands the node that looks closest to the goal, using a heuristic h(n), such as the straight-line distance to Bucharest.

It completely ignores how much it has already travelled. That makes it fast and focused, but it can be fooled: from Sibiu it picks Făgăraș (h = 176) over Râmnicu Vâlcea (h = 193) and ends up with a 450 km route instead of 418 km.
A heuristic is just an educated guess of the remaining cost; it is not the true distance.

where: estimated cost from n to the goal (e.g. straight-line distance)

cards.title: A* search
cards.hook: A* balances what you've spent (g) with what you still expect to spend (h).
formula: estimated cost of the cheapest path through n
path cost from start to n
estimated cost from n to goal
cards.memory: UCS looks Back, Greedy looks Forward, A* looks Both ways.
cards.trap: Compare f against EVERY frontier node (e.g. Timișoara 447 is still waiting), not just the newest children.
explain: A* adds the two ideas together: what the path has cost so far (g, like UCS) plus what it probably still costs (h, like greedy). f(n) estimates the total cost of the best route that passes through n.
At each step A* expands the frontier node with the smallest f. Compare EVERY frontier node, not just the newest children: Timișoara (447) stays in the frontier while Sibiu's children are compared.
If h never overestimates (admissible), A* returns the optimal route. Romania: Arad 366 → Sibiu 393 → Râmnicu Vâlcea 413 → Făgăraș 415 → Pitești 417 → Bucharest 418.

where: path cost from the start to n
estimated cost from n to the goal
estimated cost of the cheapest solution through n

cards.title: Admissible vs consistent heuristics
cards.visual: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 150" class="gsvg"><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="150" y2="30" class="ge"/><line x1="150" y1="30" x2="260" y2="120" class="ge"/><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="260" y2="120" class="ge" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="40" cy="120" r="14" class="gn"/><text x="40" y="124" class="gl">n</text><circle cx="150" cy="30" r="14" class="gn"/><text x="150" y="34" class="gl">n′</text><circle cx="260" cy="120" r="14" class="gn goal"/><text x="260" y="124" class="gl">G</text><text x="80" y="65" class="gw">c(n,a,n′)</text><text x="225" y="65" class="gw">h(n′)</text><text x="150" y="140" class="gw">h(n) ≤ c + h(n′)</text></svg>
cards.hook: A* is only guaranteed optimal if the heuristic is honest about remaining cost.
formula: h(n) ≤ c(n,a,n′) + h(n′) for every successor
tree-search A*: admissible h; graph-search A*: consistent h
example: SLD is admissible: a straight line is never longer than a road route.
If h(A) = 10, c(A,B) = 2, h(B) = 5: 10 > 2 + 5 → NOT consistent at edge A→B.
cards.memory: Admissible = optimistic. Consistent = optimistic at every single step.
cards.trap: 'Admissible' and 'consistent' are swapped in exam traps: consistency is the STRONGER property.
explain: Admissible means the heuristic is never too pessimistic: it never says the goal is further away than it really is. Straight-line distance is admissible because a road can never be shorter than the straight line.

Consistent is stronger: the estimate must not drop by more than the cost of a single step. Going from n to a neighbour n′ costs c; your estimate at n can be at most c plus the estimate at n′ (a triangle inequality).
Every consistent heuristic is admissible, but not the other way round. Tree-search A* needs admissible; graph-search A* needs consistent to stay optimal.

where: the TRUE cheapest cost from n to the goal
cost of the step from n to its successor n′

cheat.title: Classical Search cheat sheet
traps: Goal test on SELECTION for UCS/A*: don't stop when the goal is merely generated.
Ties: follow the stated tie-break (alphabetical here).
Greedy ignores g; UCS ignores h.
Repeated states: graph search skips explored states.
